cards.title: Each tablet keeps its own list of claimed tokens
cards.atAShow: A GM deletes a transaction. The engine frees the token, but every tablet that stays connected keeps refusing it as already scanned until someone reloads. A tablet that drops its connection during Reset All Scores comes back still holding the old claims, and refuses tokens the engine has cleared.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine decides which tokens are claimed, but each tablet holds a copy that only grows: added on scan, merged on reconnect, removed only when a scan fails. The engine's own messages also skip facts that change as a side effect of something else, such as a team created by a scan.
cards.designTerms: The Game record should own which tokens are claimed, read from the transactions. Delivery's interface is the one seam between a claim and a screen; each tablet is a Screens adapter drawing it. Today the tablet updates its copy with one hand-written step per message; a message with no step leaves it stale: no locality.

examples.text: GM deletes a transaction; every connected tablet keeps refusing the token as already scanned until it reloads.
A tablet that dropped its connection during Reset All Scores reconnects with its stale claims and refuses cleared tokens.
After a reload a tablet knows only its own claims; a rescan of another station's token shows success, then rejection.
A delete recomputes every team's score but the message carries one team's row; no screen shows the fault yet.
A scan for a team nobody added creates the team silently; no team message reaches any tablet.
Session Details freezes Teams and GM Stations at the last full catch-up, because one message adds to the list and the other replaces it.

cards.shapeChange: Before, the card let each tablet keep a list of claimed tokens. Now only the Game record decides claims, from the transactions; a tablet draws what it is sent and asks at each tap, so a delete or reset leaves no stale list.

cards.title: Service health and service state travel on separate paths
cards.atAShow: If the lighting system or the music player is down when the engine starts, the lighting and music panels stay disabled until someone reloads the tablet. If the music player dies mid-show, the health row turns red alone while the music card keeps its playing look and the progress bar keeps moving. A volume change on one tablet's audio panel never reaches the other tablets' sliders.
cards.whyItHappens: Each venue program has two facts about it: its health, in one shared health list, and its state, in its own record. The engine sends the health row when health changes, and sends a program's state only for a hand-written list of that program's events. An outage is on no list.
cards.designTerms: Equipment should own one dated record per thing the room does, behind one interface giving value, health and age, with the music player an adapter beneath. Delivery should own the one route: each fact built once for live and catch-up, labelled. Today each program's events are listed again by hand; whoever uses them must know every list: no locality.

cards.title: Engine trusts its stale picture of outside programs
cards.atAShow: A video stayed stopped for about 28 seconds because the engine held each message from the video player until the next one arrived. A false "video finished" can fire two seconds in, flipping the display back and restoring music. When the music player dies the engine still says playing and the controls stay dead until the next 15-second check. A cue with a 2-second video never completes.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine learns what VLC, the music player and the other programs are doing by reading their text or their stream of events into a saved copy that starts from a guess and carries no age. Re-reads are partial, and the video queue, cue timelines and health rows treat the copy as the program itself.
cards.designTerms: Equipment should own one picture per thing the room does, behind one interface giving value, health and age, checked against the program; VLC, the music player and a software stand-in are adapters at that seam. Show runner keeps none. Today the queue, timelines and health rows read each program's ageless copy directly: no locality.

cards.title: Nothing says what a game boundary clears or keeps
cards.atAShow: The GM ends the game and restarts the engine; the ended game comes back as the current one and player scans keep landing in it. When the game ends, a tablet that reconnects loses its history and the wall scoreboard goes blank. A once-only cue spent in game one stays spent in game two.
cards.whyItHappens: Game start, end, reset, engine restart, tablet reload and reconnect: each moment between games has its own code on each device. No table says, for each fact and each copy, whether that moment clears it, keeps it or fetches it again, and no message announces one; screens guess that a new game began when the game's id number changes.
cards.designTerms: Lifecycle should own the table of moments against facts and the one interface that moves a game from one moment to the next by that table; it alone calls every part's reset, and Delivery sends each moment as a fact. Today the session, cue, reset and tablet modules each hold their own cases: no locality.

cards.title: Boot and Reset System wire the engine differently
cards.atAShow: The GM presses Reset System to recover mid-show. The music panel goes dead until someone restarts the engine. Later, Reset All Scores sends every tablet and the TV the old transaction list, so cleared evidence comes back on the wall. The cues now hear each video and clock event twice, and the Display row stays red until Check Now.
cards.whyItHappens: Starting the engine and rebuilding it after a reset are two separate hand-written lists. The start sets up saving, the messages to screens and the passing of events to the cues in one order, with the full list of the engine's services; the reset sets them up in the other order with a shorter list, and sets some up twice.
cards.designTerms: Lifecycle should own the one path engine start and Reset System share, and alone reset each part; one start-up step, above every part, should own the one list the engine is built from, using the files, ports and settings Engine instance gives it. Today both do it by hand, each knowing every part and the order: no locality.

cards.title: Reconnect snapshot and live update are built apart
cards.atAShow: A GM reloads a tablet mid-game. The History badge stays hidden until the next scan, and a rebuilt admin panel can show the clock as --:-- until the next change. The device list flips between every device ever seen and only those connected now, depending on which message came last.
cards.whyItHappens: For each fact the engine has one piece of code that writes the catch-up a tablet gets when it connects and another that writes the live message, and six places send the catch-up with hand-picked contents. The tablet applies each by a different rule, and a restore after a reload sends screens none of the notices they wait for before they redraw.
cards.designTerms: Delivery should own one piece of code per fact, building the catch-up and the live message from each deciding part's changes; Lifecycle's restore sends the same, and Screens draws only what that interface defines. Today the code that builds the catch-up is shallow: whoever uses it must hand it every module, and five pieces of tablet code reshape what it builds: no locality.

cards.title: A reply never says which request, final or stored
cards.atAShow: Player devices upload their queued scans while no game exists. The engine answers "processed", stores nothing, and both devices delete the scans. A GM's scan that can never succeed comes back as a vague error, so the tablet resends it at every reconnect with a pop-up message each time. A slow Reset System reports failure and the new game is skipped.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine answers before, or without, saving the fact it reports; calls an unsaved batch processed; returns some failures as a named outcome and others as a vague error; and confirms a command by the command's name alone, so two quick presses cannot be told apart. Each device then decides for itself what a reply means.
cards.designTerms: Answering should own one interface, one request in and one reply out, with the two ways a device talks to the engine (a web request, or the live connection a tablet keeps open) as its two adapters; the outcome words are one fixed list every device reads, never written into its code; the Game record saves, then gives Answering the outcome. Today three reply formats leave each device its own rule: no locality.

cards.title: Engine and tests both assume they own the machine
cards.atAShow: On 2026-09-15 a small test stopped the live show's video player on the blue machine's code. In today's code the same test run kills the live engine's watcher for the video player and overwrites the files that say which programs are running. A killed engine leaves a full-screen player behind. Twenty-one groups of tests open a browser on the show TV. The health check shown to staff who log in, such as the GM, says "VLC not found" while the player runs.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine finds and ends its helper programs by fixed file names and by searching the whole machine for programs by name, as if it were the only engine on the machine. The tests take over whatever display, sound and Bluetooth exist; that a test is safe is claimed in a note in the code, never checked.
cards.designTerms: Engine instance should own every file, network port and setting this engine holds, behind one interface; the settings file, a test's settings and the trial copy's settings are adapters at its seam, and one start-up step builds every part with them. Today no such seam exists: modules write fixed files every engine shares, and stop programs by searching the whole machine for their names: no locality.

cards.title: Tablets and phones decide facts the engine owns
cards.atAShow: A GM scans a token; the result screen says Transaction Complete with points the tablet worked out itself, before the engine has answered. The engine may refuse, and the correction arrives as a small pop-up message. In a standalone game the tablet is the only judge, and its rules have gaps: a scan into a paused game shows complete and records nothing. A phone says revisited for last week's token.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine decides scoring, claims and whether a scan is allowed now, but the tablet carries its own copy of those rules, kept matching by hand, with a note in the code as the only reminder. The phone and the hardware scanner each choose a team on their own and decide on their own whether a token is new or already seen. Each device shows its own answer first.
cards.designTerms: The Game record should own every outcome a tap gets, running Game rules as one body the engine and the tablet both load. Answering's interface is the seam a tap crosses; Screens draws the reply. Today the tablet keeps its own copy of the rules, so a rule change lands in two places: no locality.

examples.text: Result screen says Transaction Complete with tablet-computed points before the engine answers; the engine may refuse.
Standalone: a scan into a paused game shows complete, records nothing and locks the token until a reload; an ended game still accepts.
A duplicate scan on the same tablet never names the team that claimed it; the tablet's own check refuses it first.
Every player scan carries a team no game declared; the engine discards it and only logs it.
A phone that played last week still says revisited for a token in tonight's game.
The tablet matches token ids loosely, the engine exactly; the tablet shows success and the engine refuses.

A sale carries the tablet's clock and a manual adjustment the engine's. The GM enters the first-burial bonus and the transfers as adjustments, so they printed nine hours away from the sales; ALN's Director Console shifts them back.

cards.shapeChange: Before, the card left the phone alone and had the standalone tablet load shared rules. Now one Game record judges every GM tap, on the engine or on a standalone tablet, and player devices draw the engine's reply, so a rule change lands once.

cards.title: Screens show a normal value when nothing is known
cards.atAShow: The venue profile fails to load; six services show as not installed, no video plays, no light cue fires, and the health panel reads a calm green 3 of 9. The GM presses Check Now on a down service and nothing visibly happens. The engine dies; the TV keeps counting down. The music card goes grey with no word that the engine is gone, and nobody at the venue notices.
cards.whyItHappens: No fact sent to a screen says whether it is known, unknown, stale or partial. The code that builds a tablet's catch-up swallows errors and sends a plausible normal value, a missing profile reads as no equipment, healthy only means a program answered, and the times of the last checks are never shown. The screen draws a normal value.
cards.designTerms: Delivery should own the label every fact carries: what it is, how old, how sure. Equipment's dated state feeds it, and Lifecycle passes on the Verdict's go or no-go. Screens draws the label at Delivery's seam. Today the interface of a sent fact carries neither status nor age, so an error crosses the seam as a normal value.

examples.text: A missing or wrong venue profile makes six services read not installed; the panel shows calm green with no sign.
Check Now on a down service gives no sign anything happened; no check time is ever shown.
If the TV loses the engine while the clock runs, it keeps counting down with no mark.
A cue with commands for a service not installed tonight skips them quietly and reports a clean finish.
The music panel gives no clear sign the music player is down; a greyed card went unnoticed at the venue.
Offline, the 101st queued scan silently pushes the oldest out on both player devices.

cards.seenLive: A greyed music card with no offline line went unnoticed at the venue.
cards.shapeChange: Before, the health list alone said whether a fact was known, unknown or stale. Now every fact Delivery sends carries that label, so the TV clock and music card show old or down as the health panel does.

cards.title: Several places answer the same question, each differently
cards.atAShow: Is a video playing has eight answers. A paused video counts as free, so a player is told their video was started while it waits, and releasing a held video plays over the paused one. Release All can stop at the first refused video. Music stays turned down after the queue is cleared. The downloaded report's two totals disagree.
cards.whyItHappens: Questions such as is a video playing, which teams exist and may the GM scan now are answered by several pieces of code or saved values, each with its own rule and its own way of being updated, so they disagree at the edges. No rule says which answerer every reader must use.
cards.designTerms: Each question should have one answerer inside the part that owns it, behind one interface every reader uses: the Game record for teams and whether the GM may scan, Equipment for whether a video plays. Today the video queue, the check on GM commands and the music volume rule each answer it alone: no seam, no locality.

Held cues and held videos are kept in two separate lists; Release All can stop at the first refused video.

cards.seenLive: The review ran the engine's code, and Check Now reported the display healthy when it had never launched.
cards.shapeChange: Before, the card wanted one answerer per question, as a part of its own. Now each answer lives inside the part that owns the fact, so Equipment says whether a video plays and the Game record says which teams exist.

cards.title: Pack edits reach each copy of the pack differently
cards.atAShow: A designer publishes a pack change and does not restart. The TV shows evidence by the new rules while the engine scores by the old. The file the engine hands out no longer matches the fingerprint in the engine's own pack list, so a scanner that checks rejects it. A tablet running a different pack is only noted in the engine's log; nothing tells the GM. The publish tells the running engine nothing.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine freezes one pack at start, yet the files it hands out are whatever is on disk now, and it re-reads the token list from disk at every request. The TV, tablet and hardware scanner each load the pack at their own moment and keep it; the phone reads its own copy. No message says it changed.
cards.designTerms: The Pack channel should own one loaded pack behind one interface: load, say which is current, hand out a file, announce a change. Each place a pack comes from is an adapter at its seam, and the Design studio reaches the engine's copy only by sending it requests. Today both the copy the engine froze at start and the files on disk under it cross the seam: no locality.

cards.title: The engine does not know who is connected
cards.atAShow: A tablet loses Wi-Fi and reloads; the engine still holds the old connection under the same station name and refuses the new one for up to about 85 seconds. Two tablets started together pick the same station name from an open list. The TV connects as if it were a GM tablet, receives every transaction and all ten kinds of service state, and discards what it does not need on its own side.
cards.whyItHappens: Whether a pass is asked for, and what a station is called, comes from a word the device sends, or from what the engine assumes when nothing is sent. Every kind of request checks separately, and none says who its audience is, so every live connection gets everything and reading the game's state needs no pass.
cards.designTerms: Connections and roles should own one interface that admits a connection by its pass and says its kind, name, rights and whether it is there; both ways of connecting are adapters at that seam. Answering checks rights once, Delivery filters by role. Today it trusts a self-declared word and each request checks alone: no locality.

cards.title: Names joining two places are kept by hand
cards.atAShow: A GM opens Team Details: the score box is wrong, GM adjustments never appear, completed groups read In Progress with a $0 bonus, while the scoreboard screen on the same tablet shows the real total. Game Activity shows Unknown, no stars, $0 for a token no player scanned first. The video Playing badge never appears, because the page never had a place to draw it.
cards.whyItHappens: A screen reads a field the fact never carries; a screen looks for a spot the page never had; a module waits for a message nothing sends; the written list of messages between the engine and the devices names messages nobody sends. Each name is written on both sides, and a wrong side yields nothing instead of an error.
cards.designTerms: Joins and proofs (since replaced by the published protocol and the test bench outside the engine) should own the check that both sides of every shared name agree; Delivery and Answering own the formats, written once, and Screens read them, so a missing side fails the developer's tests before the show. Today nothing checks the seam inside the tablet app: Team Details silently reads a value the tablet's store of game data never passes on.

cards.title: The deployed game is many parts nothing compares
cards.atAShow: Between shows, a rollback moves the engine's code back but none of the four shared code pieces beneath it, and a restart keeps serving the tablet app built before the rollback, so a bad rollback reaches the next show. A machine set up from the project's own instructions pairs a speaker that connects but is never set up for sound, because the instructions name the wrong Bluetooth setting.
cards.whyItHappens: The show machine holds the engine's code, four shared code pieces each at their own version, a built tablet app, hand-copied media, machine settings, start-up scripts and program names tied to one operating system release. Each moves by its own hand-run step, and nothing compares them afterwards, so a half-applied change goes unnoticed.
cards.designTerms: Release should own what is installed: one list, one interface to describe and check it, with the two machines' swap at its seam; Pack channel checks media by fingerprint, Venue fit names each machine's programs. Today no module owns it, so each piece moves by hand and the seam to the running machine goes unchecked.

cards.title: A green test run proves nothing about the show
cards.atAShow: This flaw shows nothing at a show; it is why the other fifteen flaws reached one. The small tests kept passing while Team Details showed the wrong score, because their stand-in had a value the real code lacks. A delete step in a full run-through test had been silently skipped, because it looked for the Team Details cards under a name the page never used. Blue's last full run skipped 62 tests, and group completion has no test on real content.
cards.whyItHappens: Test stand-ins are written by hand, and nothing compares them to the real code they stand for. A test step that finds nothing on the page, or checks only that no error appeared, passes. Every test engine runs with a switch that changes what Reset System does, so no test runs the reset the show runs.
cards.designTerms: Joins and proofs (since replaced by the published protocol and the test bench outside the engine) should own every test: each part is tested through its interface, a test stand-in is an adapter checked against the real part at the same seam, and one test per fact runs from the part that decides it to a screen, on its own running copy of the engine. Today stand-ins are checked against nothing and no test crosses that path.
